49-047.r: Bhadra → Karnataka; Bhavani Sagar → Tamil Nadu; Gandhi Sagar → Madhya Pradesh; Rana Pratap Sagar → Rajasthan.

49-048.r: Wrong pair: Tilaiya Dam — Konar; Tilaiya is on the Barakar (Koderma, Jharkhand). Sardar Sarovar → Narmada; Gandhi Sagar → Chambal; Nagarjuna Sagar → Krishna.

49-049.r: Wrong pair: Nagarjuna Sagar — Godavari; it is on the Krishna. Nangal → Sutlej; Sardar Sarovar → Narmada; Hirakud → Mahanadi.

49-050.r: Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar → Pipri, Sonbhadra district, Uttar Pradesh; on Rihand, a tributary of the Son.

49-051.r: Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar → Uttar Pradesh (on Rihand at Pipri, Sonbhadra district).

49-052.r: Betwa → Matatila; Mahanadi → Hirakud; Chambal → Gandhi Sagar; Tapi → Kakrapar.

49-053.r: Mata Tila Dam → Betwa river, Lalitpur district, Uttar Pradesh.

49-054.r: Gandak Project → India-Nepal agreement (4 Dec 1959); Indian partner states Bihar and Uttar Pradesh; Gandak Barrage built 1968-69; Nepal also gets electricity.

49-055.r: Kishau Dam → on Tons (major Yamuna tributary, Himachal-Uttarakhand boundary); primary beneficiaries Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh; other states also benefit.
49-055.c: The book gives no single answer (*): Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh are the primary beneficiaries, but the book says other states/UT also benefit.

49-056.r: Tilaiya → Barakar; Panchet Hill → Damodar; Rana Pratap Sagar → Chambal; Matatila → Betwa.

49-057.r: Rihand Project → Rihand; Nagarjun Sagar → Krishna; Pochampad → Godavari; Matatila → Betwa.

49-058.r: Dam not for irrigation → Shivasamudram (Kaveri, Karnataka), built 1902 for electricity generation.

49-059.r: Babli Project → controversial reservoir built by Maharashtra across the Godavari.

49-060.r: Doolhasti → Chenab; Gandhisagar → Chambal; Ukai → Tapi; Tawa → Tawa.

49-061.r: Malampuzha Dam → on Malampuzha river (Bharathpuzha tributary) near Palakkad; Kerala's largest reservoir; built by the Tamil Nadu government.

49-062.r: Singrauli Small Hydro Power Project → Sonbhadra district, Uttar Pradesh (two units of 4 MW each).

49-063.r: Cheruthoni Dam → on Cheruthoni river, a Periyar tributary, Idukki district, Kerala.

49-064.r: Rajasthan projects: Sidhmukh → Hanumangarh, Churu; Narmada → Jalore, Barmer; Jawai → Jalore, Pali, Jodhpur; Jakham → Udaipur, Pratapgarh.

49-065.r: Kol Dam Project → River Sutlej; built by NTPC (National Thermal Power Corporation).

49-066.r: Mandal Dam (North Koel project) → North Koel river (Son tributary), Palamu-Garhwa, Jharkhand; foundation laid by PM Modi on 5 January 2019.

49-067.r: Aliyar, Isapur, Kangsabati → all water reservoirs (Aliyar near Annamalai Hills; Isapur on Penganga, Maharashtra; Kangsabati earthen dam, West Bengal).

49-068.r: Kelo Irrigation Project (Raigarh, Chhattisgarh; Kelo is a Mahanadi tributary) → included under Prime Minister Irrigation Project.

49-069.r: States in water tribunals: Mahadayi → 3; Godavari → 5 (now 7); Narmada → 4; Mahanadi → 2.

49-070.r: Large dams, descending (among options): Madhya Pradesh > Gujarat > Rajasthan > Telangana > Andhra Pradesh. Overall most: Maharashtra, then MP, Gujarat.

49-071.r: Three wrong pairs: Ghataprabha → Karnataka (not Telangana); Indira Sagar → Madhya Pradesh (not Andhra Pradesh); Maithon → Jharkhand (not Chhattisgarh). Only Gandhi Sagar → MP correct.

49-072.r: Mangdechhu Hydropower Plant, Bhutan → inaugurated by Indian PM Narendra Modi in 2019.

50-001.r: Permaculture vs chemical farming: permaculture discourages monoculture, avoids soil salinity, relies on mulching; it works even in semi-arid regions (answer 1, 2, 4).

50-002.r: Zero tillage advantages: wheat sown without burning residue, paddy seeds sown directly without nursery, soil carbon sequestration → all three.

50-003.r: Fertigation (fertilizer via drip water) → controls water alkalinity, raises nutrient availability, cuts leaching; not rock/super phosphate (precipitates) → answer 1, 3, 4.

50-004.r: Eco-friendly agriculture in India: crop diversification, legume intensification (fixes nitrogen), tensiometer use, vertical farming → all four.

50-005.r: 'The History of Indian Agriculture' → M.S. Randhawa (Mohinder Singh Randhawa), key figure in Green Revolution research.

50-006.r: India: 15 agro-climatic regions (resource development) and 20 agro-ecological regions (NBSS&LUP); statements I and II swap these numbers.
50-006.h: C before E, 15 before 20: Climatic 15, Ecological 20.
50-006.c: The explanation repeats statement III as a fact, but (b) needs III to be false, and it is: the cold arid eco-region (Ladakh) is only a part of the much larger Western Himalayan agro-climatic region.

50-007.r: Upper Gangetic agro-climatic region → central and western UP; irrigation intensity about 131% (>130%), cropping intensity about 142% (>140%) → both true.

50-008.r: Agro-ecological regions of India → 20 (National Bureau of Soil Survey); each uniform in physiography, climate, growing period, soil.

50-009.t: Don't confuse 20 agro-ecological zones with 15 agro-climatic regions.

50-010.r: P. Sengupta and Galina Sdasyuk (1968 Census monograph) → India divided into 60 micro agricultural regions.

50-011.r: Dry zone of India: agrarian economy (A true); large scope for second Green Revolution through irrigation (R true); R does not explain A.

50-012.r: Seed Replacement Rate constraint → demand-supply gap of quality seeds for low-value, high-volume crops. National Seed Policy 2002 exists; private firms do supply (answer 3 only).

50-013.r: First agricultural university → G.B. Pant University of Agriculture and Technology, Pantnagar (as UP Agricultural University), inaugurated by Nehru, 17 November 1960.

50-016.r: Safe storage → grain moisture at harvest not above 14% (FAO standard).

50-017.r: Land use in India ≈ net area sown 47%, forests 23%, others 30% (2022-23: net sown 45.88%, forest 23.49%, others 30.63%).

50-018.r: Double cropping → two crops on the same land at different times within one year (e.g. wheat, then corn); needs a long growing season.

50-019.r: Mixed farming → crop cultivation and animal rearing together, with equal emphasis.
50-019.t: Don't confuse mixed farming (crops + animals) with mixed cropping (two or more crops in one field).

50-021.r: Parallel cropping → two non-competing crops grown together in parallel rows, e.g. Wheat + Mustard.

50-022.r: Sikkim → hilly, mostly forest; less than 10% of land available for agriculture (so most land left out of farming).

50-023.r: Indian agriculture: dependence on nature, low productivity, crop diversity; NOT large farms (small and marginal holdings dominate).

50-024.r: Low productivity of Indian agriculture: overcrowding, small land holdings, traditional practices → all of these.

50-025.r: Green Revolution technology → turned traditional farming modern and scientific (irrigation, specialized seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, machinery). Book: A and R true, R not the explanation.
50-025.c: The book treats R ('no big social and environmental costs') as true; the Green Revolution is widely known for such costs, so (c) 'A true, R false' is the stronger answer.

50-026.r: Not a cause of low farm productivity: cooperative farming (a development measure). Causes: population pressure on land, disguised unemployment, small holdings.

50-027.r: Average operational holding (Agriculture Census 2015-16): Punjab larger than Rajasthan. Rajasthan, Maharashtra, UP lead in total operated area. Book's answer: Rajasthan.
50-027.c: Doubtful key: by average holding size Punjab is well ahead of Rajasthan (Agriculture Census 2015-16), so (a) Punjab fits better; Rajasthan, Maharashtra and UP lead only in total operated area.
